utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just prior to that, I might indicate that again this morning we've been having the -- the laptop issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed about the laptop issue and I have spoken personally to the technician who promised that where the problem seems to be the copying of the files stored on the hard disk, copying to the -- that he would do whatever he could to assist Mr. Krajisnik in getting it there and it seems to be caused by the change of the laptop and different systems of storing and writing on a CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, that's the -- that's the current issue with the laptop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has our full attention. Anything else at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom. At the same time, I'd like to draw the attention of the parties to the agenda we have for the housekeeping matters later on this morning. I hope that it's clear that if we do not work efficiently we might not finish with the housekeeping which would finally result in having to deal with the remainder of the housekeeping matters tomorrow morning. The more efficient we are, the smaller the chance that we would have to come back tomorrow morning for that reason alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I must say from my perspective, Your Honour, I think it's very unlikely that we would need to come back tomorrow morning. My cross-examination won't take all that long and I'm sure we'll have an ample opportunity to deal with the housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Quite, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas who is counsel for the defence of Mr. Krajisnik. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mehinagic. Now, Mr. Mehinagic, you indicated in your evidence that you met with Mr. Krajisnik twice in relation to this very important Tuzla-Zvornik railway project; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And these are in fact I think the only two occasions on which you've met with Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And they were both, of course, business meetings that did not touch upon any political issues.

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the duties of the speaker of the parliament or president of the Assembly, do you have -- I see your microphones are just being adjusted there. I think the microphones have now been adjusted. Now, in relation to the duties of the speaker of the parliament or the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I take it you have an awareness of the basic functions of that position?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Including, basically, firstly, that he presides over the Assembly and allows various deputies to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that matters are proposed for voting by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, that Mr. Krajisnik only has one vote just like all the other deputies; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the vote is cast, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now -- and obviously, are you aware that he could not of course control the agenda that went before the Assembly, that matters that were proposed for the agenda by the various deputies' club whether it be SDA, HDZ, SDS had to be put on the agenda whether he agreed with them or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law, and under the procedure, the speaker of the Assembly had significant impact on the items to be placed on the agenda and he would be the one to sign off the agenda. And I disagree with what you just stated about the agenda. Nothing could have been inserted into the agenda that had not been approved by the speaker of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just getting back to that, Mr. Mehinagic, I'm sure we're not in dispute at this point. The actual signing of a matter to go on the agenda was basically a formality. I mean, he couldn't stop something coming to the parliament, could he?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything further about this other than what I've just stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So obviously you don't put yourself forward as some sort of expert on the political structures and powers of the speaker or the president of the Assembly of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a figure that was positioned quite highly in the period up until 1990 in the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was familiar with the system by virtue of my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course --

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why in general terms, the matters stood as I've just described them. Now, if you wanted any further information, you would have to consult experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, and that's the point, Mr. Mehinagic. Now, in relation to one matter you've indicated in your statement, and that is Mr. Krajisnik signing off on regulations and laws, again, would you -- I take it you'd agree with me that that was of course a formality, the formal position of the president of the Assembly meant that there was a signature there. Are you able to offer anything in relation to that or, again, is this within the limits of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my current high position in the administration and -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina today, I would give you the following information: The authority of Mr. Krajisnik to sign off any pieces of legislation or other regulations that he was authorised to sign under the regulations, his signature meant that all the previous legislative procedure had been implemented and that only his signature now was needed in order to make a given piece of legislation effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now again just in relation to that, Mr. Mehinagic, again I don't think we're in dispute here but of course that is the formal position on signing off from a matter from the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a formal procedure governed by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely. Now, you've mentioned that -- of course, currently you're in a high position, but prior to, I think you mentioned in one of your answers prior to 1990, of course that was the previous regime, that was of course under the communist regime that you're referring to; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the regime that was in power in the former SFRY until 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Everything's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, under the previous regime, it was extremely important to have good contacts with high profile people in the hope of exerting influence, that would be a correct assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is always important to have good contacts with high-profile people in whatever regime.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that's probably right, Mr. Mehinagic. Now, of course -- and of course in relation to your project, you wanted influential people on the side of the project; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I am, by nature, a person who favours transparency and I was governed by this principle in my dealings with highly positioned people.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Mehinagic, and that, of course, is important and appropriate. Now, in relation to your actual reporting in relation to the project, I think you've mentioned here in paragraph 6 of your statement that you regularly reported to the Prime Minister Jure Pelivan and to the Minister of Finance in relation to the progress of the project but of force you didn't formally or in any way report to Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course basically your business meetings with him were to ensure that he, as a high-profile person, would support the project; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think you knew that he had a good relationship with the Croatian -- Bosnian Prime Minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only natural for me that a speaker of the Assembly and a Prime Minister should be on good terms but I did not really pay much attention to that. I thought that the positions that they held were relevant. I, as the person responsible for very a significant project, had to have good contacts but with either of them -- with both of them, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in response to one of Mr. Margetts's questions yesterday, that's at page 10 for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, you were asked by Mr. Margetts why was it important specifically for support to be provided by Mr. Krajisnik? And included in your answer was this: "By virtue of his position, Mr. Krajisnik was after the president of the republic, the second ranking figure in the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In view of his position, I thought it important to regularly inform him thereof. And, secondly, he played an important role in the adoption of a budget for the construction of the railway because such a project was always tabled before the Assembly and they decided upon it and Mr. Krajisnik was speaker of that Assembly." Now, just in relation to the -- what you've indicated there about the ranking, it would be true to say, would it not, Mr. Mehinagic, that that was basically your perception of the ranking; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to an official hierarchy or a perception of a position was that you would have -- the person number one would be the president of the Presidency, then the speaker of the parliament, and the Prime Minister, and that was a formal view of matters, not my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course that view is very much a formal and symbolic view rather than a view based on actual power; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this time, and today, I always thought that this was how the hierarchy was under the law and under the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But obviously, Mr. Mehinagic, as you've quite fairly conceded, you don't put yourself forward as some sort of expert on political structures; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to move on to another topic and that is just in relation to people in Zvornik prior to the outbreak of the war. It would be true to say, would it not, that prior to the break-up of the war, many residents left Zvornik, both Serbs and Muslims; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many residents of Zvornik left the town but those who were leaving at that time were predominantly Serbs and I can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course you would agree with the statement that there were, of course, Muslims and Bosniaks as well even though you indicate that you say that they were predominantly Serbs leaving at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could we perhaps first clarify what the witness exactly meant by "at that time"?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You've heard His Honour indicate "at that time." What did you mean in your answer when you gave that phrase "at that time"? Would you like me to read your answer again to you or are you happy to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my return from Belgrade on the 3rd of April in the afternoon hours, I saw a column of Serbs leaving Zvornik and heading towards Loznica in their own vehicles and with their families. At the same time, I listened to Loznica and Valjevo radio broadcasts saying that the Serb populace is in danger and that they should be mobilised in that respect. This is something that I, myself, experienced. There were only isolated cases of Croats and Muslims leaving, sometimes also with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated there that the radio was saying that the Serb populace was in danger and that they -- when you say --

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in precisely those terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: All right. That the Serb population was in danger, the radio was saying that, and Serbs were leaving as a result; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was listening to Valjevo and Loznica radio stations and I was shocked by what I was hearing because the people there could not possibly have known what was going on in Zvornik. And this was a way of them deceiving their listeners.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In any event, you were aware of -- prior to the break-up of the war, that there were families, both Serb and Muslim, who actually left Zvornik to go to Serbia. You are aware of that, are you not?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to another matter that you've mentioned in your statement and that is in -- I think it's -- yes, paragraph 90 of your statement, you don't need to have it before you. It's just in relation to the -- perhaps I've misnumbered it. In any event, you were aware of an incident whereby a JNA officer Mihajlo Stojanovic was killed on April the 5th, 1992. You're aware of that incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't this officer Stojanovic but rather another person, a warrant officer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name.

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I'm familiar with the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just in relation to that, to your knowledge, who attacked the officer that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to explain this in several sentences, if we have enough time for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure we do but we can take it step by step. To your knowledge, who attacked the officer that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer was the one who opened fire first, so I can't really say that he was attacked. I saw with my own eyes the document brought by Captain Dragan Obrenovic. This was just a piece of paper torn from a notebook. This was a handwritten statement by the JNA soldier who, at the time, was in the Zvornik hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've indicated in your statement that there was this incident and -- yes, you've indicated in your statement that to your knowledge, it was subsequently -- well, quite directly it was subsequently established that the first to shoot in this incident was the JNA Warrant Officer Second Class Stojanovic. And you've indicated there that "I stayed in the office of the chief of police and after a few hours, Obrenovic returned to the station. At this time he brought a handwritten statement of the soldier who was injured in the incident and this statement recorded that Stojanovic had fired the first bullet." So that's the matter that you're referring to now in your evidence that's already in your statement. Now, what I'd like to know is, leaving aside the fact that you say your knowledge is that Stojanovic had fired the first bullet, who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please correct the statement if it does state that it's Stojanovic, because his name was Stanojevic, Warrant Officer Stanojevic. On that day, there was a fair at Stapna and there were many people gathered there. Since an incident took place that very afternoon at Kalesija, the JNA was tasked to pass through Stapna on their way to Tuzla and not through Kalesija. The column found it hard to advance through the multitude of people gathered there for the fair. I realised that at some point, some of the people perceived the column passing through Stapna at the time as a provocation and stopped the column from proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "stopped the column"?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to say anything about this. I was in Zvornik at the time and I'm just telling you what I heard. I wasn't there. But the information I have is reliable because following this event, I went to the Zvornik police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Are you aware that -- just getting back to what you were saying about Stanojevic, I think perhaps the confusion is my pronunciation of the name. I think it's actually correct in this statement, it's just that my pronunciation of B/C/S sometimes leaves something to be desired and makes the names sound different. Now, just in relation to this incident, are you aware, firstly, that Stanojevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that a squad leader and lieutenant were wounded?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that one soldier was captured and he was bound and kept as a hostage?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't remember all these details now, but that's what the situation was. Others who were there fled and sought shelter or refuge in the nearby woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Now, just in relation to that, you say that your information is that Stanojevic had fired the first bullet. I understand that. But who fired after that, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, both sides fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "both sides," on one side, you have the JNA, who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sapna, the place where the fair was organised is a Muslim place, and obviously, some Muslims must have opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, any questions arising from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, counsel for the Defence took you to paragraph 29 of your statement relating to the radio announcements you heard on the 3rd of April, 1992, and the convoy of Serbs you saw leaving Zvornik in their personal cars and you've indicated this morning that they were leaving for Serbia. Did the Serbs that left on the 3rd of April, 1992, remain in Serbia permanently?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 3rd of April in the afternoon between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m. because that was the time when I was coming back from Belgrade where I had had lunch with a former Presidency member, Sreten Mijatovic. I was flabbergasted when I saw that column because it was an indication that the attack -- an attack of Zvornik was probably imminent. To my knowledge, some of those people went back on Monday morning. Quite a few families, on the other hand, stayed in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You were also referred to matters relating to this incident that occurred in Sapna and that was a controversial incident when it occurred. Did you take any steps to clarify the factual situation relating to what occurred in that incident?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was very much against any violence and I implement measures in order to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Why did you consider it important to clarify the factual situation relating to that event?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced that it was essential to establish who provoked the incident in order to deal with the consequences in a legal way and it would make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you involved in discussions with Serb representatives and other Muslim representatives in relation to this matter and --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll let you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'll finish my question there then if -- I see my learned friend rising to her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'll ask you this, were you involved in discussions with representatives of Serbs and other Muslim representatives in relation to the Sapna incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honours, I do object because this is not actually a matter that arises in re-examination. My cross-examination was directed specifically to the events in question and his knowledge of the events and not directed to the broader question of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. There was a clear suggestion in your questions, Ms. Loukas, that this may have triggered other matters and in that respect, it's relevant to hear whether any negotiations specific on this matter took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So Mr. Mehinagic, I'm just asking you whether negotiations -- well, in the course of the negotiations you've described, was the Sapna incident a subject that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, prior to that, I had insisted and it was organised for soldiers, arms, and vehicles to be gathered and brought back to Zvornik. Secondly, following my insistence and my assistance, of course, the president of the Assembly contacted the corps commander with regard to the incident, and he apologised. And thirdly, at the People's Defence Council meeting, we decided that proper light should be shed on incident at Sapna and everybody agreed and they were all bound by that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you say "everybody agreed," was that everybody in attendance at that meeting and, if I may refer you to your statement, I'm referring to the list of attendees at paragraph 41 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object to this form of re-examination. The -- in re-examination just as in evidence in chief, the Prosecution is prohibited from leading and when you say "'Everybody agreed,' was that everybody in attendance at that meeting, and may I refer you to your statement," Your Honours, I would submit that that's leading in relation to that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the words "everybody agreed and they were all bound by that agreement" are the words of the witness and this is simply a clarifying question so that the witness can specifically refer to the people by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clarifying and a bit leading. Yes, you are drawing the attention to a certain group of people. But when you said that "everybody agreed," could you tell us who you had in mind with "everybody"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA, the representatives of the Crisis Staff of the SDS, the representatives of the legal authorities of the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say JNA and the representatives, are you referring to a specific occasion or -- because I take it that not the whole of the JNA agreed with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a conclusion which was formally reached at the meeting of the People's Defence Council of the municipality of Zvornik on the 6th of April. I did not have such a conclusion to be approved previously in talks with people, I arranged for it to be agreed to or also on behalf of General Jankovic and Colonel Tacic who was in charge of the armoured and mechanised brigade so that was the basis for all parties reaching that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was the significance of the all of the parties being agreed in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Captain Dragan Obrenovic got to the police station, he threatened that he would destroy Sapna. When he came back and there was a statement from the soldiers, he had already changed his mind. What was significant to me was for the incident to be clarified in a fair and honest way and for things to be patched up so as to avoid that being used as an excuse to attack Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, please, you had said in Zvornik, the previous social situation and ethnic situation before the times we are relating to lately was of harmonious living together of all ethnicities. Do you have the impression that that was only an exception in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina or do you know of other municipalities in which this situation was similar, that is, that Muslims and Serbs and Croats were living together without problems one against the other?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole was characterised by harmonious interethnic relations. And things started to get worse, especially with the rise in nationalism and the expansionist ambitions promoted by Slobodan Milosevic's movement and following the elections whereby national parties won in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, that leads me to another question which is: How is said then that this kind of fighting against ethnicities started in this very moment, something should have happened before then. Some historical evolution was already underneath when this moment arrived, so is it the case?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my opinion, it could not have happened earlier because proper and harmonious national policies were in place. Apart from that, cohesion forces of Yugoslavia were the dominant ones and it wasn't possible for any major upset to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: So how is it that Zvornik became so different from the other municipalities just in this very moment, because it's plainly evident that in other opstinas, in other municipalities, the situation of ethnic fronts fighting was very general and very common, how was it that in Zvornik, you felt that it was different or -- can you mention besides some other municipalities in which the situation could be similar to that of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could mention quite a few municipalities, first and foremost Tuzla in our immediate vicinity, and then Brcko. And I think quite a few other municipalities, for example Lukavac, Gracanica, Gradac. And I think that generally speaking we've always had stability in terms of national relations all the way up until 1990 in all municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, please. You've talked of the first session of the Council of National Defence, I would like you to provide some explanation on the composition, the membership of the Council for National Defence and its role. In the general administration of the municipality, was it provided for or was it an ad hoc creation?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a body which was -- the existence of which was enshrined in law and it existed in all municipalities. It was headed always, according to legal provisions, by the president of the Municipal Assembly and other members were the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly, the secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, the secretary of the Municipal Secretariat of the Interior, the Chief of Staff of Civil Protection, the commander of the Territorial Defence, and that's the basic structure of this council. As to the duties and obligations, the council had the decision-making powers when developing the defence plans for the municipality in exceptional circumstances, including the threat of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the period that we're mentioning, before 1991, 1992, was the National Council often in meetings? Did it have any opportunities to meet?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That body never met very often. They used to meet once or twice a year and the reason for the meeting being convened on the 6th of April, 2004 [sic] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was the fact that the representatives of SDS boycotted the meetings of the General Assembly, Municipal Assembly, and all the representatives of the SDS basically boycotted the Municipal Assembly. And because of that and the barricades, having been set up in -- on the territory of our municipality, the economy ground to a halt and the business leaders, some of us, asked for things to be sorted out and we wanted to resolve the situation. And the representatives of the SDS accepted that it should be in the form that it should be done through this council, the National Defence Council, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your answer, you indicate that the council met regularly once or twice a year before the period. Why would the council meet at the time when there was no climate of hostility, why would the council meet and what would they do?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would meet to agree on decisions, for example, military exercises which tended to happen once every year or once every two years in the area and where units from Zvornik would be participating. They would meet to make some administrative decisions with regard to the entire defence system. And they met on the basis of the orders coming from higher up, from the level of the Republic to discuss matters of this sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to put the following question to you,

utterances.speaker: MR. MEHINAGIC
utterances.text: I understand from your testimony that you now feel deceived that the JNA, who you expected to protect the population, took part in what you called "the attack on Zvornik." This participation of the JNA, could you tell us perhaps a bit in more detail what other groups, entities, units, whatever you'd call it, were involved together with the JNA in the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things I know for sure are that an armoured mechanised battalion of Tacic's brigade participated in this attack and the commander was Dragan Obrenovic and that there were also formations of the Territorial Defence of the municipalities, Mali [Realtime transcript read in error "mainly"] Zvornik and Loznica participating as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these Territorial Defence formations mono-ethnic or were they multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't testify about that. On that morning when Zvornik was attacked, at 5.30 I got a call from the president of the Municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Assembly to come to SUP and to meet with three saboteurs who had been arrested and that was a sure sign of an imminent attack and when I got there, they showed me their military papers, their military IDs and those were JNA IDs and their headquarters was at Pancevo. At a later stage I saw a statement on the basis of which one of these people was Vojin Vuckovic who later was tried for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to rise to my feet and interrupt the witness's answer but at page 20, line 23, the transcript appears to record that -- what does record "the formations of the Territorial Defence's, mainly Zvornik and Loznica," I think that may be an error and if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was "Mali," as far as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I heard, understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's my understanding as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no disagreement about "Mali" instead of "mainly." There was a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the basis of the tapes that we saw yesterday, on the basis of many of the accounts, people in Serbia ranging from Seselj to Arkan were giving you a list of all the units that were participating there. And I did say yesterday that I left Zvornik under fire at around 4.00 p.m. on the 8th of April, and there was a lot of machine-gun and gun fire from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mali Zvornik and Loznica, were they --

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mali Zvornik and Loznica are municipalities in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In -- then as far as paramilitaries are concerned, apart from what you saw on the television report, did you receive at that time any information about the involvement of paramilitary units in the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called Serb Territorial Municipality Zvornik Units from my point of view, legally speaking, were a paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us on what you base this opinion?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base this opinion on documents that I had been shown here in this court on the basis of which the Serb Democratic Party activated those units and that was totally illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you know whether they were in one way or the other under the command of any regular troops or forces?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason why these activities of the Territorial Defence were illegal was that there was an official order from the federal minister, General Kadijevic, for the Territorial Defence not to be used and not to be mobilised for any purpose whatsoever. So it was a totally illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any police forces or units involved in the attack on Zvornik, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the reports I saw on television where Arkan and Seselj were speaking, that was my source of information and there were these units from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about the attack on Zvornik and you gave a specific time on when that started. All the units or forces you just mentioned, did they become active at approximately that same moment?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 8.30, the attack was launched in the direction of the village of Lipovac and that part of the outskirts of Zvornik, so from Bijeljina directed at Zvornik. Later on in the course of the day, fire was opened from the direction of Serbia as well and those were the two lines of attack from Bijeljina and from Serbia. Of course I can't judge what units they were except that I recognised the artillery of the self-propelled battalion of the JNA, and grenade launchers, 120 millimetres; the mortars, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may have understood that I'm trying to find out whether there was any coordination between those units that participated in the attack on Zvornik. Could you give us any additional facts which would either support or contradict a coordinated action between these units? If you don't have any of these facts, please also tell us.

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except from the general belief on the basis of all the facts that I had at my disposal, yes, that there was coordination, but apart from that, I have no other specific information to give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Finally, if you -- a question: If there is a dinner, who would you place left and who would you place right of the one who presides over that dinner? Is there any hierarchial order on who to place to your right-hand side and who to place to your left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a hierarchy. On the right-hand side, you would usually place the person holding the highest rank. On the left-hand side would be the person ranking next in order to the one seated on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you made the table order, if you did, or if you were involved in any way, was this the underlying thought in placing persons at the dinner where -- I think it was the opening or - let me just find it - the lunch you had at the Hotel Drina on the 5th of March, 1991. Was this in your mind or are you aware of this being in anyone's mind when the seating at the table was prepared?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I was the most responsible person for this particular lunch and I was the one who composed the order of those to be seated at the table. And of course I could not have missed placing the high-ranking or the highest-ranking person to my right and the next in order to that person to my left. Therefore yes, I was the one who organised that particular detail and I kept these things in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my last question is about the budget of the project where you said that it was Mr. Krajisnik who would have to table the budget in the Assembly. Did you have any reason at that time to believe that if you would not have the specific assistance of Mr. Krajisnik, that it would not be properly put on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- this warrants to be explained further. The Republican Assembly passed the annual resolution which was, in actual fact, an agenda of the most important activities to be undertaken in the course of that year. I found it very important for that comprehensive project to be included in the resolution. Secondly, the Assembly adopted the Republic's budget and I thought it important that a proposal where the project should be given due notice be actually passed from the executive council to the parliament. This, of course, regardless of the fact that the project had quite independent funds, however, at this point in time, there was a plummeting inflation and one had to take this into consideration. Rumours circled that these -- that the budget could be used by Serb nationalists, that the project could be used by Serb nationalists to connect Serb Krajinas with Serbia. I did not wish to take these arguments into account at all because I thought that the project itself had overriding importance that goes beyond these interests. That is why I did not fear that the Serb deputies might reject the proposal. But I did not see the speaker of the Assembly as a Serb but rather as the speaker of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From all what you tell us now, it appeared there was no specific interest to speak with the speaker of the Assembly about it. You say the project was important enough, one could not expect any objection by Serb parties to it. Nevertheless, you spoke with Mr. Krajisnik about the project. It's not entirely clear to me what the importance then was.

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The importance lay in the fact that the person number one in the Republican Assembly should be fully informed about the project, and that it be ensured that this particular person continues to support the project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would his support be anything else than the support of any of the other members of the Assembly, because you said it would be on the agenda anyhow because it was an important project so it was just one out of how many votes for support?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matters are never as simple as they might seem when it comes to important issues. The speaker of the Assembly is man number one in the legislative branch of government. He presided over the body that was to decide on the agenda of the activities to be carried out in the Republic that particular year. He presided over the body that adopted the annual budget of the Republic. This role is a very significant one and far from ceremonious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I understand your testimony well, are you saying that he had this key position and therefore his opinion could be of influence, or even would be of influence on the opinion of others?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any need to put any additional questions to the witness in relation to the questions raised by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, you were questioned about the units present in Zvornik, that is the military units. In paragraph 30 of your statement you said that on the 4th of April, 1992, you learned that the Serbian Territorial Defence of Zvornik had been mobilised and also Exhibit P647 dated the 5th of April, 1992 is, in fact, an order issued for the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence. Do you know which units were mobilised pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this order on TV Belgrade on the 4th of April in the evening at 10.40 p.m. I was very much shaken by it. On my arrival here, a written order dated 5th of April was shown to me and it confirmed my belief that this was, in fact, what took place. Full mobilisation of units was carried out in secrecy so I am not, myself, aware, I was not aware of units being mobilised. I do know, however, that units were mobilised and I have a statement by a JNA lieutenant who talked of cases where soldiers who refused to respond to a call-up were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know whether those units that were mobilised were involved in the events from the 8th of April, 1992, that is, the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the information I received --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but again, Mr. Margetts has asked this question as a matter apparently arising from His Honour's questions, he's asked: "Do you know which units were mobilised pursuant to this order?" Again, Your Honour, the same question is asked, that is, Your Honour, I object to the question that doesn't seem to me to take the matter any further for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the same question. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, do you know whether those units that were mobilised were involved in the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the information I received, and according to all the public information available about the event, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, any further questions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, just getting back to the events of the 8th of April which you set out in your statement and you were asked some questions in relation to that by Their Honours, it seems to me that on the 8th of April you have this early morning meeting in relation to four of Arkan's men, correct, that's the first thing that basically happens on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a meeting, I was called to come over to the SUP to see the saboteurs that were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then subsequently, you do attend a meeting with the representatives of the SDS and then Arkan slaps the representatives of the SDS in that meeting that's later on that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any meetings with the SDS that day because the attack started as early as 8.30 a.m., and I only had intense contacts with General Jankovic and Colonel Tacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was with Pasic where the SDS representatives were slapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I'm having difficulty understanding how this arises from Your Honour's questions and if my learned friend could give some indication at least of the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour specifically asked what occurred on the 8th of April and I'm trying to ascertain, and Your Honour asked some pointed questions in regard to coordination. And I'm trying to elicit the specific factual evidence of what the witness was actually saying on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that not the 8th of April as a whole was triggered by questions of the Bench but certainly coordination between the units or formations involved in the attack is an issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehinagic, so -- and you very wisely, on that day, left Zvornik with your family at 1600 as you indicate in the statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It wasn't very wisely that I did it. Actually, I am ashamed, thinking about it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, since you responded to it, Ms. Loukas included some comments in her question which she should not have done and you don't have to respond to those comments. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, and I withdraw the comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehinagic, what I'm just trying to ascertain here is you mentioned in your statement there that you saw that Zvornik was attacked from Serbia and that you knew that the Territorial Defence from Loznica and Mali Zvornik had been mobilised and were attacking, but in terms of what you were actually able to observe, yourself, firsthand, on that day as to what was occurring, that was pretty limited in terms of the time you had outside being able to observe; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IZET MEHINAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. Mali Zvornik and Zvornik formed part of practically one and the same community. It's just 100 metres across from the Drina. And I was able to see it with my own eyes, it's a small town. Secondly, I used to go to Mali Zvornik quite often. On the 6th of April in the afternoon and I believe that this is stated in my statement, I was at the headquarters of Dragan Obrenovic's command and I pleaded with him that if Zvornik came under attack, that he protect my child, that he take care of it. There was also Despotovic, commander of the TO in Mali Zvornik there who was in full military gear and he told me that his units had been mobilised. I, myself, saw mortar batteries at the Vlaske Njive, as it is called, across the Drina River, this could not be concealed, it was for everyone to see. I saw the positions taken by these units in Mali Zvornik and in Serbia, one could see it -- they were as if laid out on the palm of one's hand. And these are the sources of my information.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Witness. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinagic, this concludes your testimony in this court. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, it's quite a distance. You have answered the questions of all parties and of the Bench. It's important for the Chamber to hear the witnesses who have been present at the time when the events occurred; therefore, thank you, and we wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was an honour for me to be able to contribute to the establishment of truth and justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mehinagic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, we'd like to deal with the exhibits at this moment but then stop and after the break deal with the other housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just mention something -- good morning, Your Honours. May I just mention something immediately before the break, which is: One of the items on the housekeeping list relates to confidentiality in relation to certain passages connected with Mr. Mandic whose evidence, of course, has generally been released and openly. The -- Your Honour, we will -- we would have time, the issues have been sufficiently considered by Mr. Tieger and myself, we don't agree, Your Honour, that is the position. Mr. Tieger has narrowed it down to a certain number of passages but I, in relation to those passages, I still do not agree. Your Honour, there would be time and we'd suggest it's the appropriate way of dealing with - it is why I mention it now so there's a little bit of notice - but to deal with this today, Your Honour. There's plenty of time likely to be in hand to deal with it and the most convenient course would be to deal with it in a -- by oral submissions today, that has the advantage, of course, that then the public knows what the issues are and Mr. Krajisnik can hear what the issues are and we can get it done today. And then of course it's for the Chamber to make its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could your oral submissions be such that they could be public?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It strikes me that that would be a bit awkward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's not entirely the point because whether the submissions are in public or in private, they could still be dealt with today. If it really becomes necessary to have submissions in private, it's the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just say it's good for the public to know what the issues are, therefore my question was whether we could deal with them in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of them would be bound to be capable of being dealt with in public as to the principles that we're dealing with. If it were necessary for some of them to be dealt with in private, that doesn't undermine the essential point. But it's also important, Your Honour, that as far as possible we do not deal with these things in -- in writing which means translation for Mr. Krajisnik to deal with them and it's precisely the kind of issue which, without putting the label of debate on it, it's precisely the kind of issue where an intelligent tripartite exchange of questions and answers between the Trial Chamber and the parties is likely to lead to a more satisfactory result than doing it in a compartmentalised way by a written submission from one party and a written submission from another party then the Trial Chamber considering that. It is precisely the sort of issue which doesn't lend itself and require, we submit, to be properly dealt with, and we do have the opportunity to do it today, Your Honour. It's wasteful, in effect, for us to go away and deal with it in writing when there's clearly going to be enough time to deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you oppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll leave it to the Chamber. However, I have to offer my view that I believe that the issues that are genuinely pertinent to this conflict at the moment can be and, for the most part, have been resolved and -- not resolved, but reduced in writing, lend themselves to identification and clarification in written form, any oral submissions that might be required beyond that I would imagine would be extremely limited. So as a general matter, I don't share the enthusiasm for a public debate, if that's what it was described at on this issue. I think the issues are relatively simple and can be clarified and have been clarified in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't say public debate. Mr. Tieger's compressing two things. But Your Honour, let's -- may I say this, I have been pressing Mr. Tieger for a long time. We don't agree about this, that's -- and I, as advocate, as Mr. Krajisnik's representative, I'm not prepared to agree with that. We don't agree but I have been pressing Mr. Tieger for a long time to give me the reasons. I've had about ten lines are from him months ago which don't really tell me the position. Your Honour, this is the opportunity for Mr. Tieger to explain - the matter's been on the table for ages - to explain very clearly to the Trial Chamber and at the same time to me what the basis is for his saying that these -- these matters should remain in private session and then I can deal with them. This is the proper way of dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we hear from the parties what parts are still in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have been made available to the Trial Chamber in an e-mail, the clarification was made to counsel in a direct discussion several weeks ago conducted on the balcony which I'm sure he will recall if he puts his mind to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Precisely. It becomes, it becomes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was not a single line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, we've --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- of new information given to me on the balcony. I was given the same reference I already had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we come romantic with balcony scenes, I must have overlooked the e-mail. So we can identify clearly how much time would you need, Mr. Stewart, to explain why this -- these specific aspects should be public?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, it's the other way around, Your Honour, this is precisely what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Tieger, if you would have to explain why you would keep them confidential, how much time would you need to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A very short time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give -- could you be more precise, 3 minutes would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll take 3 minutes.

utterances.text: Yes. I think it was filed yesterday in the afternoon. Then I move to the next subject which is the decision to be delivered by the Chamber on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for 92 bis witnesses. This is a decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Rule 92 bis witnesses. The motion which is partially confidential, was filed on the 31st of January, 2005. Pursuant to Rule 75 of the Rules, the Prosecution originally sought an order that the identities and identifying information of 22 92 bis witnesses not be disclosed to the public. The Defence filed its response on the 24th of February, 2005, opposing the motion in its entirety. On the 10th of March, the Trial Chamber invited the Prosecution to provide any supplementary information on the objective basis underlying each application for protective measures. On the 22nd of March, the Prosecution filed this supplementary information with respect to three witnesses. It also notified the Chamber that it was withdrawing its request for protective measures for seven witnesses. The Defence filed its response to this supplementary information on the 8th of April, and this decision therefore concerns the 15 92 bis witnesses for whom the Prosecution still seeks protective measures. The Prosecution, in the confidential annexes to its motion and its notification of supplementary information, briefly sets out the reasons on the basis of which protective measures are sought in respect of each witness. It also incorporates by reference, its submissions, as set out in a separate protective measures motion filed on the 11th of March, in relation to a recent UNHCR report. That report describes the current security situation affecting persons who have given or may give evidence before the Tribunal. The Defence, in its response to the motion and to the supplementary information, notes generally that the subjective fears of a witness are not the proper basis for a grant of protective measures unless there is evidence showing a real risk to the security of the witness or his or her family. The Defence makes specific submissions on the inadequacy of the reasons provided by the Prosecution to justify protective measures for ten of the witnesses. Further, the Defence argues that it is incumbent on the Chamber to insist upon being provided with all relevant information, and to be satisfied that all reasonable inquiries have been made to obtain that information before making its ruling on the motion. The Defence submits that these requirements have not been met in the present case. Turning to the applicable law, the Trial Chamber notes that in its submissions, the Defence has consistently sought to apply to motions for protective measures the higher standard required for temporary relief from disclosure whereby disclosure of a witness's identity is delayed until a set deadline. That standard is inapplicable here. The Chamber has stated the correct standard for protective measures in a number of recent decisions. The parties seeking the measures must demonstrate the existence of an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become publicly known that the witness gave evidence. It will usually be sufficient for a grant of protective measures if a party can show that a threat was made against the witness or, for example, that there exists a combination of the following three factors: One, the expected testimony of the witness may antagonise persons who reside in the territory where the crimes were committed, for example, by implicating those persons in crimes; two, the witness or his or her family live in that territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory; and three, there exists an unstable security situation, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. In addition to questions of security, where an application for protective measures concerns sexual assault victims, there is a long line of authority, which is based on considerations of privacy, providing that the identity of such victims will be protected if those victims so request. The Defence is correct in stating that the Chamber may, at its discretion, make further inquiries in relation to an application for protective measures. However, as set out in a decision of this Chamber dated the 20th of September, 2004, the Chamber is not under any obligation to inquire further. The Chamber will normally be satisfied once the objective basis for a security risk that I have just described is demonstrated. In the present case, the Chamber has requested, and has obtained further information. Noting the problems associated with contacting some witnesses, the Chamber is also satisfied that the Prosecution has made all reasonable inquiries to obtain information relevant to the motion. I will now proceed to give the findings of the Chamber in respect of each witness. The fear expressed by Witnesses 3 and 122 is supported by the fact that both have been subject to threats of a serious nature. Witness 3 received a threat directly related to giving evidence to the Tribunal which has been reported to the police in his country of residence. Witness 122 appeared in the media in Republika Srpska and subsequently was repeatedly threatened by persons known and unknown to the witness. The Chamber rejects the argument of the Defence that there is insufficient information about the nature of those threats. The Prosecution has shown that there is an objectively grounded risk to the security of these witnesses or their families. The Chamber therefore grants the requested protective measures in respect of these witnesses. I now turn to the witnesses 128, 114, 12, 281, 428, and 588 who have all expressed fear for their own safety or that of their families if it becomes publicly known that they gave evidence to this the Tribunal. Two of these witnesses live in or close to the area in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina where the crimes they describe in their evidence were committed; one witness has family in that area; and three have described concrete plans to return there. The evidence of these witnesses, all of whom allege crimes committed by local Serbs, may antagonise the persons implicated in those crimes, exposing each witness to a real risk of retaliation. Moreover, Witness 128 implicates political and military personnel in serious crimes, and some of the persons implicated in crimes by Witness 428 remain in positions of authority in the relevant area. Taking into account the general security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which remains unfavourable to those giving evidence to the Tribunal, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has established the existence of an objectively-grounded risk to the security of all six witnesses or their families. The Chamber therefore grants the requested protective measures in respect of these witnesses. A psychiatrist's letter has been submitted in respect of Witness 215, stating that she suffers from severe post traumatic stress disorder as a result of her experiences during the war and that any "direct contact with her traumatic memories" poses a serious threat to her very fragile state of health. The Chamber is not prepared to accept even a small risk that as a result of giving evidence, such a witness might be identified and subsequently confronted in a way that is likely to revive her memories and thus gravely to endanger her health. For this reason, the Chamber grants the requested protective measures in respect of this witness. Witness 133 has expressed fear for family who still reside in Bosnia without providing any further information. The Chamber recognising that in response to its request for supplementary information about this witness, the Prosecution diligently attempted to contact him and was unable to do so. However, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, as set out in a number of the Chamber's recent decisions clearly states that the burden rests on the party seeking protective measures to justify the grant of those measures. In the case of Witness 133, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has provided insufficient evidence of an objectively grounded risk to the security of the witness or his family should it become known that the witness gave evidence. The Chamber therefore denies the requested protective measures in respect of Witness 133. In light of this decision, the Prosecution may, of course, withdraw his statements from evidence. Should it choose not to do so, and should it succeed in contacting the witness at some future stage, the Chamber would consider any renewed application for protective measures. Witnesses 436, 141, 148, 086, and 109 are all victims of sexual assault who give evidence about those assaults. The Chamber recalls that there is a long line of authority in this Tribunal based on considerations of privacy, which states that victims of sexual violence may be accorded protective measures where they so request. The Chamber therefore rejects the argument of the Defence that this, of itself, is an insufficient basis for a grant of protective measures. Considering that there is a need to show special consideration for persons testifying about sexual violence, the Chamber grants the requested protective measures in respect of these witnesses. The Registrar is instructed to file the 92 bis statements of those witnesses to whom protective measures have been granted confidentially.
